function.name: copy_path
function.description:
Copies a file or directory, preserving the original; directories are copied recursively. More efficient than reading then writing contents. Returns confirmation with the destination path.

Import past work: source_path accepts '@<session-id>/<rel>' to copy from your OWN past session (find the id with recall, browse with list_directory). destination_path never accepts '@' - past stays read-only, imports land in the current session directory. The destination must not exist yet; nothing is overwritten.

After import the file is fully local: read_file (images included), terminal, mint_public_link all work on it. You can peek a past text file without importing (read_file takes the same '@' form); importing is what makes it workable (terminal, edit_file, images).

Limits: max 200 MB / 200 files per call; symlinks refused.

source_path.description: File or directory to copy, relative to the session working directory (absolute paths inside it accepted). '@<session-id>/<rel>' imports from a same-user past session.

destination_path.description: Where to place the copy inside the CURRENT session directory (relative, or absolute inside it). '@' paths are rejected here. Must not already exist.

function.name: db
function.description: Execute operations on the session's SQLite database (data.db in the session working directory). The database file is isolated per session and auto-created on first use. For inserting rows (especially batches), prefer op=insert which avoids writing SQL by hand; use exec/query for DDL, updates, deletes and complex SQL.

op.description:
Operation type:
- exec: run a write statement (CREATE / UPDATE / DELETE / ALTER / DROP), in a transaction
- query: run a read-only statement (SELECT / WITH), returns an array of rows
- insert: insert one or more rows from row objects (structured, no SQL needed, one transaction)
- tables: list all tables with row counts
- schema: show column definitions for a table

sql.description: A single SQL statement. Required when op is exec or query. Use ? placeholders for parameterized queries to avoid SQL injection; multiple statements are rejected.

params.description: Values bound to the ? placeholders in order. Used by op=exec/query only. Booleans are stored as 0/1.

rows.description: Array of row objects for op=insert. Each object maps column names to values; all objects must have the same keys.

function.name: edit_file
function.description:
This is a tool for applying edits to an existing file.

Before using this tool, use the `read_file` tool to understand the file's contents and context.
To create a new file or overwrite an existing one with completely new contents, use the `write_file` tool instead.

When copying text from `read_file` output into `old_text` or `new_text`, strip the line-number prefix and the tab after it, and keep the original indentation exactly.

Matching rules:
- `old_text` is first matched exactly. If there is no exact match, a fuzzy match tolerating minor whitespace and formatting differences is attempted.
- If `old_text` matches more than one location (overlapping matches count as separate locations), the edit fails. Include enough surrounding context to make it unique; avoid very short or repetitive `old_text`.
- If no match is found at all, the edit fails. For very large files the fuzzy stage degrades to per-line whitespace-insensitive exact matching; the error message says so — do not retry the same text, locate with `read_file` by line numbers or use `terminal` with sed.

To delete whole lines, put the exact line(s) in `old_text` and set `new_text` to an empty string — matched whole lines are removed cleanly together with their line endings (a trailing newline in `old_text` makes no difference).

Edits are applied in order. If one edit fails, the edits before it are already written to disk and the file has changed: the error message tells you how many were applied. You must call `read_file` again before retrying; do not reuse the previous `old_text` values.

path.description: Path of the file to edit, relative to the session working directory. Absolute paths are also accepted. '@' paths are rejected here — copy a past file in with copy_path first.

edits.description: List of edit operations to apply sequentially. Each edit finds `old_text` in the file and replaces it with `new_text`. If any edit fails, the edits before it remain applied.

old_text.description: The text to find in the file. Matched exactly first, then fuzzily (whitespace / minor formatting differences tolerated). Provide enough context to make the match unique; short or repeated snippets are reported as ambiguous. A trailing newline, if present, is stripped before matching. For whole-line deletion, put the exact line(s) in old_text and pass an empty new_text.

new_text.description: The replacement text. Use an empty string together with a trailing-newline-free `old_text` to delete a whole line.

function.name: fetch
function.description:
Fetches a URL and returns its content as Markdown. Only http and https are supported; if the scheme is omitted, https is assumed.

HTML pages are converted to Markdown. JSON, XML, plain text, and Markdown responses are returned as-is. Binary responses are not returned — only their HTTP status, content-type, and size.

The response always starts with a line `HTTP <status>`, followed by the body. Check the status line: a non-2xx status means the fetch did not succeed, even if body content is present.

Returned text is capped per call (default 12000 chars; a call may raise it with `max_chars`, hard cap 64000). When truncated, the tail hint gives the total length and the `offset` to continue from — re-call with that `offset` to page through WITHOUT re-downloading. Most pages fit in the first window; only page further when you actually need more.

Targets that resolve to private/loopback addresses are refused (SSRF guard). Redirects are followed up to 5 hops, each hop checked.

url.description: The URL to fetch. Must be http or https; if no scheme is given, https is assumed.

offset.description: Character offset into the converted page body, for continuing a truncated fetch. Use the offset value given in the previous truncation hint. Requires no re-download.

max_chars.description: Max characters to return for this call. Optional; raise only when the default window clearly cut off content you need. Values above the hard cap are clamped.

function.name: handoff
function.description:
Hand off from the advising phase to the execution phase. Call this when the task brief is ready. The system stores your `brief` as the task brief and switches to execution. There are three cases:

- ready: The requirement is clear enough to execute.
- user_skip: The user explicitly asks to stop planning with you ("just move on", or similar) — this skips only the advising conversation, it never waives the user's later confirmations. Do not call this on tone or mood alone — only on explicit signals.
- user_stuck: You have asked 2-3 rounds and the user is still not providing key information, and they seem to want to move on.

When reason is not "ready", the `brief` must carry the user's own words plus every open question under a Missing section — the executor is required to ask the user these before acting. Do not invent a methodology or generic plan.

brief.description: The task brief content, in Markdown. Follow the structure described in your system prompt.

title.description: A concise title for this conversation, in the user's language (3-7 words, or 6-14 Chinese characters). Straight to the title: no quotes, no prefix like "Title:".

function.name: lab
function.description:
Unified entry point for calling any available tool by name.

Call a tool:
  lab(tool: "<name>", args: {<arguments>})

The target tool's arguments go inside `args` as a JSON object. Omit `args` for tools that take no arguments.

Discovering tools:
  lab(tool: "help")                          → list all tools with a one-line description each
  lab(tool: "help", args: {tool: "<name>"})  → full description and parameter schema of <name>

An unknown tool name also returns the list of available tools.
Nested lab calls are rejected; inner tool errors surface unchanged.

Calling a tool directly and calling it through lab are equivalent. When the tool you need is already in your tool list, call it directly. Use lab to discover or reach tools that are not in the current list.

tool.description: Name of the tool to call, or "help".

args.description: Arguments for the target tool, matching its own schema (look it up with lab(tool: "help", args: {tool: "<name>"}) if unsure). Omit for tools that take no arguments.

function.name: list_directory
function.description:
Lists the entries directly inside one directory (one level, like `ls`): folders and files, sorted; hidden entries (starting with '.') omitted; max 200 per call, go deeper with a deeper path.

path is relative to the session working directory (absolute paths inside it accepted); empty/omitted lists the current task directory.

Past sessions: '@<session-id>/<rel>' lists a PAST session's own directory, same user only (read-only view). Find the id with recall op=search. In '@' mode entries print as complete '@<session-id>/...' paths, ready to feed copy_path.

path.description: Directory to list, relative to the session working directory. Absolute paths accepted. '@<session-id>/<rel>' lists that past session's directory (same user only; id from recall).

function.name: mint_public_link
function.description:
Create a short-lived (default 30 minutes, server-configurable 1min-24h), publicly reachable URL for a local file, so an external service that cannot authenticate can download it. The link works repeatedly until it expires; re-mint for a fresh one.
Use this when another tool or API needs to fetch a local file by URL. Returns the URL as plain text on a single line.

path.description: Path of the file to publish, relative to the session working directory. Absolute paths inside the session working directory are also accepted.

function.name: profile
function.description: Maintain the current user's profile — stable facts that persist across conversations and get injected into the context of NEW sessions (the current session's injected copy is frozen). Ops: list (read the live profile), set (honorific or industry, single short value), add (append preference tags), remove (delete exact preference tags). Rules: only record what the user has clearly stated or asked to be remembered (form of address, domain, stable output/work preferences); never guess personality, never store one-time task parameters; brief tags beat essays. Preference is a 、-separated tag list (each tag ≤15 chars, ≤24 tags, ≤300 chars total; overflow is rejected — consolidate or remove first). When unsure what is already recorded, op=list returns live state — trust it over memory.

op.description: list = read live profile; set = single-value honorific/industry; add/remove = preference tags.

honorific.description: op=set: how to address the user (≤20 chars, e.g. 王工). Pass empty string to clear. Exactly one of honorific/industry per call.

industry.description: op=set: the user's industry/domain (≤20 chars, e.g. 金融). Pass empty string to clear.

tags.description: op=add/remove: preference tag list, e.g. ["偏好简洁回复", "图表中文标注"]. Matching is exact text.

function.name: read_file
function.description:
Reads the content of a file.

Text files: each returned line is prefixed with a line number right-aligned in a 6-character field, followed by a tab, then the line content.

Cross-session peek: `path` accepts '@<session-id>/<rel>' to read a text file from your OWN past session, read-only (find the id with recall op=search, browse with list_directory). It is a look, not an import: nothing lands in your session directory, so `terminal`, grep and `edit_file` cannot see it, and past images are refused. When you need to work with a file or view a past image, `copy_path` it first (its `source_path` takes the same '@' form). '@' is never accepted by `write_file` or `edit_file`.

Large text files (roughly over 16 KB) are not returned in full: you get an outline listing top-level symbols (or Markdown headings) with line numbers instead. The outline IS a successful response — do NOT retry the same call without a line range; use the outline line numbers with `start_line` / `end_line` to read specific sections. If no outline can be extracted, a first-1KB excerpt is returned instead. Supplying `start_line` or `end_line` disables outline mode.

Image files (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, TIFF) are returned as visual content you can analyze directly, but only if the current model supports vision; otherwise a text placeholder is returned — that placeholder is not an error. The tool result itself carries a text notice only; the actual image pixels arrive in a separate user message right after the batch of tool results: that message lists per-image labels matching each image to its read_file receipt, then the image blocks in receipt order, and asks you to briefly describe each image before continuing. Never re-read an image already delivered in the current turn; if pixels never arrive, tell the user instead of retrying. Very large images (roughly over 50 MB) are skipped, and images may be downscaled (long edge ~2000 px, re-encoded as JPEG) before being returned.

Binary files are not returned as text; a short notice is returned instead. Text files over 32 MB cannot be read by this tool — use `terminal` (grep -n / head / sed -n).

path.description: Path of the file to read, relative to the session working directory. Absolute paths are also accepted. '@<session-id>/<rel>' reads a same-user past session's file (text only; past images need copy_path first).

start_line.description: Optional 1-based line number to start reading from.

end_line.description: Optional 1-based line number to end reading at (inclusive). Must be >= start_line. Supplying either bound disables outline mode.

function.name: recall
function.description:
Access your long-term memory: the work diary. Each finished session leaves one short fragment (a few dozen chars) there, headed by its source session id; fragments are kept permanently, but only the newest were injected at session start - recall reads the whole archive on demand. Read-only.

op=search  Fuzzy keyword match over ALL fragments, best first. Primary entry when the user vaguely recalls something - you cannot know what you have forgotten.
op=days    Index of days that have entries (newest first) - when the user remembers roughly WHEN but not what.
op=day     Full fragments of one day.

Returns are plain text: search hits print '--- date (match%) ---' then the session id and fragment; days list dates with entry counts; day lists fragments. A miss comes back as a short 'no records' line - a normal answer, not an error.

op.description: Recall operation; what each op does is in the tool description.

query.description: op=search: keywords; space-separated words rank best (e.g. '身份证 水印'). Chinese and English, case-insensitive; Chinese tolerates partial phrases.

count.description: op=search: max fragments to return (default 10, max 30).

date.description: op=day: the day to open, YYYY-MM-DD exactly as shown by op=days.

function.name: schedule
function.description:
Manage scheduled tasks (alarms). Call this ONLY when the user explicitly asks for something to run periodically or at a specific time.

Model: each task lives on exactly one session (at most one per session) and is addressed by its task id — the home session id shown by op=list, format 'task-YYYYMMDD-NNN'. Omit id to act on THIS session's task. At each trigger the prompt is delivered to the task's session as a new user message; prior history is archived first. Cron times are Asia/Shanghai (UTC+8). Returns are compact key=value blocks; failures come back as 'Error: ...' and are safe to retry after fixing arguments.

op=get     Optional id.
op=list    No arguments. All tasks of the current user across sessions, one block per task starting with its id — pass that id straight to get/update/delete; never ask the user to switch sessions.
op=create  THIS session only; id is rejected. Requires cron_expr, prompt and brief; optional script.
           Side effect: the creating session retires into the task's dedicated home — it gets archived and the user's next message starts a fresh session.
op=update  Optional id. Requires at least one of cron_expr, prompt; other fields unchanged.
op=delete  Optional id. Cancels the task.

id.description: Task id as shown by op=list (the session the task lives on). Omit for THIS session's task. Not allowed with op=create.

cron_expr.description: Standard 5-field cron expression, e.g. '0 9 * * *' for 09:00 daily. Runs must be at least 1 hour apart — denser expressions are rejected (not silently adjusted). Required with op=create; optional with op=update (recomputes next run).

prompt.description: Self-contained instruction delivered as the only input at each trigger (prior history is archived). Each run's closing reply plus newly written artifact files are automatically pushed to the user via WeChat, so do not wire a webhook/email push into the prompt. Required with op=create; optional with op=update.

brief.description: One short plain line (<= 40 characters; CJK counts as 1) saying what the task accomplishes, e.g. 'collect and produce a daily news PDF report'. Goes into the assistant's long-term memory diary. Required with op=create; immutable afterwards.

script.description: Optional for op=create. A script filename (relative to the session working dir) meant to carry this task's routine so triggers reuse muscle memory instead of redoing everything. Supplying it means: distill the workflow into that script NOW (language, invocation and how the prompt references it are yours to decide). Never validated at create or trigger — a missing/broken script surfaces as a runtime error in the trigger turn. Immutable afterwards.

function.name: skill
function.description:
Use the skills installed on this server. A skill is a directory under the skill root whose SKILL.md defines its purpose and input_schema.

op=list  No arguments.
op=get   Requires name.
op=run   Requires name; input_args optional (default {}).

op=list: lists all installed skills with a one-line description each, read live from the skill root; use it to choose among skills or to confirm what is installed. An empty skill set returns an empty list — that is not an error.
op=get: returns the full raw SKILL.md (front matter included): purpose, input_schema, and usage notes. Call it before op=run with a skill you have not used in this conversation. A nonexistent skill returns an error.
op=run: executes the skill with input_args validated against its input_schema (a validation error names the missing fields). The entry script receives a JSON string as its only CLI argument, so input_args must be a JSON object.
- Returns the skill's combined stdout+stderr as plain text after it exits; exit 0 with no output yields '（无输出）'. A non-zero exit raises an error containing the output and [exit code: N].
- Direct output files via arguments: relative paths in input_args are resolved against the session working directory; do not rely on the skill's cwd.
- Default timeout 120 seconds: the process group is killed and the error includes partial output collected so far (a timeout is not a skill failure).

name.description: Name of the skill (subdirectory name under the skill root directory). Required with op=get and op=run.

input_args.description: Dictionary of input arguments for the skill. Keys and values should match the skill's input_schema (call op=get first if unsure). Example: {"input": "file.md", "output": "out.pdf"}. Used only with op=run; omit it for skills that take no arguments.

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Executes a shell one-liner and returns combined stdout/stderr output.

- Run commands relative to the session working directory. Use the `cd` parameter to specify a different directory if needed.
- Do not use shell substitutions or interpolations (e.g., `$VAR`, `${VAR}`, `$(...)`, backticks). Resolve values yourself first.
- Do not pipe output to `head` or `tail`; use the `head_lines` and `tail_lines` parameters to limit what is returned while keeping full output visible to the user. Both can be combined: the result is the first head_lines lines, a blank line, then the last tail_lines lines.
- Avoid commands that run indefinitely (servers, watchers). For long-running commands, set `timeout_ms`.
- Each invocation starts a new shell; do not rely on state from previous calls.
- If a command may open a pager or editor, disable it using environment variables (e.g., `GIT_PAGER=cat`, `EDITOR=true`).

command.description: The shell one-liner to execute. Do not include shell substitutions; use literal values.

cd.description: Optional working directory for the command. If omitted, runs in the session working directory. Accepts relative or absolute path.

timeout_ms.description: Optional maximum runtime in milliseconds. If exceeded, the process is killed.

head_lines.description: Return only the first N lines of output to the model. The user still sees full live output.

tail_lines.description: Return only the last N lines of output to the model. The user still sees full live output.

function.name: write_file
function.description:
Creates a new file or overwrites an existing file with the given content.

Parent directories are created automatically, so the path does not need to exist beforehand.

Overwriting replaces the file's entire content irreversibly. If the file already exists, read it first, or use `edit_file` for targeted changes instead.

Text is written as UTF-8. To produce binary files, use `terminal` instead.

path.description: Path of the file to create or overwrite, relative to the session working directory. Absolute paths inside the working directory are also accepted. '@' paths are rejected here — the past is read-only.

content.description: The entire content to write. Required — pass an empty string to create an empty file; omitting it is an error.
